Criehaven (Ragged Island), Maine
Hi mom!
Criehaven is a historical and alternative name for Ragged Island, an unorganized territory in Knox County, Maine.
In ordinary it is real-world reference material: the fictional blackwell-island off Cape Cod is a natural carbon copy of Ragged Island’s landmass.
This page records the real place; how much of it carries over is settled on blackwell-island > The Criehaven Template.
The island the story uses
Criehaven is a geographic template only: blackwell-island copies Ragged Island’s natural landmass, the same 28 miles offshore, and none of its man-made features. Which features carry over, and how the FBPRC’s paper cover imitates Criehaven’s ownership shape, is recorded once, on blackwell-island > The Criehaven Template.
Identity and Status

Criehaven (pronounced “cree-haven”) is an alternative name for Ragged Island, an unorganized territory in Knox County.
Criehaven was formerly a plantation comprising Ragged Island (just south of Matinicus Isle in outer Penobscot Bay), Matinicus Rock (to its southeast), and Seal Island (to its northeast; Seal Island National Wildlife Refuge).
It surrendered its organization in 1925 and reverted to unorganized territory, but the name persists.
It is a small rocky island in Penobscot Bay, not Casco Bay; the Harpswell “Ragged Island” is a different island.
It lies about 28 miles off Midcoast Maine and about 7.5 miles south of Matinicus.

Naming

Charts from 1754, 1776, and 1819 show “Ragged Ass Island,” which McLane suggests may render “Racketash,” Abnaki for “island rocks.”
Mid-19th-century charts call it Ragged Island; Matinicus lobstermen reportedly still say “Ragged Ass” “out of perversity.”
It calls itself the “Island of Lobsters,” and claims to be the farthest offshore inhabited island on the East Coast (a promotional claim, unverified).

Geography and Area
Census Bureau figures for the Criehaven location:

The territory is overwhelmingly water; the island itself is about 0.7 square miles (or 350 acres by a 1994 Maine Times figure).
Natural geography: a network of trails accessible from a stone beach; an undeveloped southern end with a long mossy trail to the tip; a rocky, harbor-centered landscape; and phosphorescent “fiery water” around the island at night.
Harbor and Access
The harbor is “a tight little rock-lined harbor” with “little space for visitors and no room to anchor,” protected from all directions except the north and northwest.
Anchoring is impossible because the bottom is solid granite, crossed by steel cables that hold the fishing fleet’s moorings; when those are full, Matinicus guest moorings are used.
A breakwater, damaged by storms in 1978, has a beacon at its end.
What was built (real island only)
Fishermen’s homes; houses scattered on the rocks; a dozen tiny lots framing the harbor, most with a workshop and a wharf; the Criehaven Library, “half museum, half library, and half community center”; a dock trolley; and a tiny airstrip.
None of these exist on blackwell-island.
History





























DateEvent1849Robert Crie and Harriet Hall move to Ragged Island1879According to chronicler Charles McLane, Robert Crie owns the whole island1896Crie incorporates Ragged Island as the plantation of Criehaven1925The plantation dissolves and reverts to unorganized territory1941The school closes
Crie prospered in farming and lumbering, and kept a general store for many years alongside fishing, sheep raising, and farming.
According to McLane, after Crie’s death the community’s “vigor” was gradually drained by natural disasters and changing times.
After the school closed, the departure of year-round families cost the island its general store and post office.
A “lively summer community of fishermen and vacationers” continues, but there has “rarely been year round habitation in recent years.”
Community

Described as Maine’s only seasonal fishing community.
A few lobstermen and families live there in summer; no one year-round.
The 2010 Census counted one person.
Seasonally there are ten lobster-fishing families and ten non-fishing families; some stay all summer, some part of every week.
A 1994 source says about 90 percent of the island was owned by one person, Richard Krementz of New Jersey.

Cultural References
Ragged Island was the home of writer Elisabeth Ogilvie and inspired her “Tide Trilogy”; writer Dorothy Simpson lived on Criehaven for many years; a fictionalized Criehaven is the setting of the web series “Ragged Isle.”
Real-world details, not story canon.
Limitations
The reference material is Wikipedia-style and web notes, not primary archival evidence; several historical claims rest on Charles McLane.
Natural features may transfer to Blackwell Island; man-made features should not, unless they are explicitly adopted.
The evidence is moderate: the external record agrees on the broad geography, but some details are dated, anecdotal, or second-hand.
